JOINT REBUTTAL TESTIMONY 
OF 
PETER BLAZUNAS, LANCE SCHAFER 
AND 
HANHAN HAMMER 
I. 
INTRODUCTION  
1 
Q.  
Please state your name, title, business address, and provide your professional 
2 
background and relevant experience. 
3 
A. 
[Blazunas] My name is Peter Blazunas, and my business address is 293 Boston Post Road

Inc (“Concentric”). I am the same Peter Blazunas who sponsored Direct Joint Testimony 
6 
filed on February 23, 2026, in this proceeding. 
7 
[Schafer] My name is Lance Schafer, and my business address is 293 Boston Post 
8 
Road West, Marlborough, MA 01752. I am a Senior Project Manager with Concentric. I 
9 
am the same Lance Schafer who sponsored Direct Joint Testimony filed on February 23, 
10 
2026, in this proceeding.

[Hammer] My name is Hanhan Hammer, and my business address is 293 Boston 
1 
Post Road West, Marlborough, MA 01752. I am a Senior Project Manager with Concentric. 
2 
I am the same Hanhan Hammer who sponsored Direct Joint Testimony filed on February 
3 
23, 2026, in this proceeding.   
4 
[Blazunas, Schafer, and Hammer] Our professional background and relevant 
5 
experience was provided in Exhibit No. PTO-0002 of our Direct Joint Testimony filed on 
6 
February 23, 2026, in this proceeding. 
7 
II. 
BACKGROUND 
8 
Q. 
What is the background for this proceeding? 
9 
A. 
[Blazunas, Schafer, and Hammer] On December 18, 2025, the Commission issued its 
10 
order in PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217, at P 193 (2025) (“Order”). In 
11 
the Order, the Commission found that PJM’s Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) 
12 
“is unjust and unreasonable because it does not contain provisions addressing with 
13 
sufficient clarity or consistency the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to 
14 
generators serving Co-Located Load and Eligible Customers taking transmission service 
15 
on behalf of Co-Located Load.”1 Specifically, the Commission found PJM’s Tariff “unjust 
16 
and unreasonable because it does not include types of transmission service that reflect 
17 
Eligible Customers taking service on behalf of Co-Located Loads that are willing and able 
18 
to limit their use of the transmission system under certain conditions.”2
19 
The Commission ordered PJM to offer three new forms of transmission service 
20 
under its Tariff, and identified these three new forms of transmission service as: (i) Firm 
21 
1
Order at P 2. 
2
Id.

Exhibit No. PTO-0005 
Page 3 of 31 
Contract Demand transmission service (“Firm Contract Demand Service”); (ii) Non-Firm 
1 
Contract Demand transmission service (“Non-Firm Contract Demand Service”); and (iii) 
2 
interim, non-firm transmission service (usually referred to as “Interim NITS”). The 
3 
Commission also established a paper hearing to determine the just and reasonable rates, 
4 
terms, and conditions for these new transmission services. The paper hearing process 
5 
provides for initial briefs, responses to initial briefs, and replies to those responses. 
6 
III.  
PURPOSE OF TESTIMONY 
7 
Q. 
What is the purpose of your testimony?  
8 
A.   
[Blazunas, Schafer, and Hammer] The purpose of our testimony is twofold. First, we 
9 
provide additional detail regarding a proposal to impose financial penalties for Eligible 
10 
Customers3 taking service on behalf of Co-Located Load that make unreserved use of the 
11 
transmission system. Second, we respond to certain criticisms made by parties in their reply 
12 
briefs regarding the rate designs proposed by the PJM Transmission Owners4 for the three 
13 
new transmission services required by the Order. This includes our responses to testimony 
14 
3
All capitalized terms that are not otherwise defined herein shall have the meaning set forth in the PJM Tariff 
or Amended and Restated Operating Agreement of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
4
For purposes of this testimony and the accompanying reply brief, the PJM Transmission Owners are: 
American Electric Power Service Corporation on behalf of its affiliates, Appalachian Power Company, Indiana 
Michigan Power Company, Kentucky Power Company, Kingsport Power Company, Ohio Power Company, Wheeling 
Power Company, AEP Appalachian Transmission Company, AEP Indiana Michigan Transmission Company, AEP 
Kentucky Transmission Company, AEP Ohio Transmission Company, and AEP West Virginia Transmission 
Company; The Dayton Power and Light Company d/b/a AES Ohio; Dominion Energy Services, Inc. on behalf of 
Virginia Electric and Power Company d/b/a Dominion Energy Virginia; Duke Energy Business Services, LLC for 
Duke Energy Kentucky, Inc. and Duke Energy Ohio, Inc.; Duquesne Light Company; East Kentucky Power 
Cooperative; Exelon Corporation on behalf of its affiliates Atlantic City Electric Company, Baltimore Gas and Electric 
Company, Commonwealth Edison Company, Commonwealth Edison Company of Indiana, Inc., Delmarva Power & 
Light Company, PECO Energy Company, and Potomac Electric Power Company; FirstEnergy Service Company, on 
behalf of its affiliates American Transmission Systems, Incorporated, Jersey Central Power & Light Company, Mid-
Atlantic Interstate Transmission LLC, The Potomac Edison Company, Monongahela Power Company, Keystone 
Appalachian Transmission Company, and Trans-Allegheny Interstate Line Company (collectively, the “FirstEnergy 
Companies”); PPL Electric Utilities Corporation; Public Service Electric and Gas Company; Rockland Electric 
Company; and the Southern Maryland Electric Cooperative.

Exhibit No. PTO-0005 
Page 4 of 31 
accompanying the reply briefs filed by Constellation Energy Generation, LLC 
1 
(“Constellation”) and Vistra Corp. (“Vistra”) that address the PJM Transmission Owners’ 
2 
Grid Reliance Charge proposal. 
3 
IV. 
FINANCIAL PENALTY PROPOSAL 
4 
Q. 
Should unreserved use penalties apply to Eligible Customers taking Firm Contract 
5 
Demand Service, Non-Firm Contract Demand Service, or Interim NITS on behalf of 
6 
Co-Located Load? 
7 
A. 
[Hammer] Yes. Robust penalty provisions are a necessary component of the new services 
8 
required by the Commission. First, and most importantly, any penalties must be sufficient 
9 
to meaningfully deter Co-Located Load customers from exceeding their contract demand 
10 
or Interim NITS limits and making unreserved use of the transmission system. Because 
11 
network upgrades are planned and built only to accommodate load covered by Firm 
12 
Contract Demand Service or NITS, it is crucial that Co-Located Loads respect their 
13 
contractual limits, including any related curtailment or other instructions from PJM. This 
14 
concern is particularly acute because many of these arrangements will likely involve 
15 
substantial amounts of load—hundreds, if not thousands of MW—being served by on-site 
16 
generation but still connected to the grid. If these limits are not respected, the reliability 
17 
consequences to the system—and to existing customers that rely on the reliable operation 
18 
of that system—could be severe. 
19 
Q. 
Has PJM proposed any penalties? 
20 
A. 
[Hammer] Yes. PJM’s Initial Brief includes a table summarizing PJM’s proposed 
21 
operational penalties applicable to Eligible Customers taking service on behalf of Co-
22

Exhibit No. PTO-0005 
Page 5 of 31 
Located Load.5 PJM explains that it also supports a financial penalty in addition to its 
1 
proposed operational penalties and that it intends to work with the PJM Transmission 
2 
Owners to explore a financial penalty framework.6 Specifically, PJM states that 
3 
“[u]nreserved use penalties should apply to Eligible Customers taking Firm Contract 
4 
Demand Transmission Service, Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, or 
5 
Interim NITS on behalf of Co-Located Load.”7
6 
The PJM Transmission Owners agree with PJM that the imposition of financial 
7 
penalties is appropriate, as any penalty regime should rely on both operational 
8 
consequences and complementary financial penalties. Although the PJM Transmission 
9 
Owners anticipate that operational penalties will provide the primary deterrent against 
10 
Eligible Customers serving Co-Located Load exceeding their reserved transmission 
11 
service use, financial penalties will play a valuable role in enhancing this deterrent as well 
12 
as ensuring the market and other ratepayers are made whole if an Eligible Customer serving 
13 
Co-Located Load exceeds its contract demand or Interim NITS limits. 
14 
Q. 
Do the PJM Transmission Owners have a proposal for an appropriate penalty charge 
15 
to address any unreserved use of the PJM transmission system by an Eligible 
16 
Customer taking transmission service on behalf of a Co-Located load?
17 
A. 
[Hammer] Yes. In addition to PJM’s proposed operational penalties for failure to curtail 
18 
upon instruction, the PJM Transmission Owners propose to apply financial penalties in 
19 
instances in which an Eligible Customer taking service on behalf of Co-Located Load 
20 
exceeds the authorized transmission service limits, as described in more detail below. The 
21 
5
PJM Initial Brief, Docket Nos. EL25-49, et al., at 41 (filed Feb. 23, 2026). 
6
Id. at 50. 
7
Id. at 51.

Exhibit No. PTO-0005 
Page 6 of 31 
authorized transmission service limits will include any reduction based on curtailments 
1 
directed by PJM. 
2 
Q. 
Do the PJM Transmission Owners propose that the Commission adopt a separate 
3 
“Failure-to-Curtail” Financial Penalty?  
4 
A. 
[Hammer] No. The PJM Transmission Owners are not proposing that the Commission 
5 
adopt a separate “failure‑to‑curtail” financial penalty. Instead, failure to curtail should be 
6 
treated as a form of unreserved use and addressed through a single, unified unreserved use 
7 
financial penalty framework. Failure to curtail inherently results in unauthorized use of the 
8 
transmission system. As such, it is part of unreserved use and does not warrant a distinct 
9 
penalty mechanism. However, as indicated above, the financial penalties proposed here 
10 
will account for any failure to curtail by factoring any curtailments directed by PJM into 
11 
the determination of an Eligible Customer’s authorized transmission service limits.  
12 
Q. 
Please describe the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposed financial penalties for 
13 
unreserved use. 
14 
A. 
[Hammer] The PJM Transmission Owners propose a financial penalty charge structure 
15 
for unreserved use with two components: (1) a base penalty charge, which applies to each 
16 
individual hour in which the reserved transmission service limit is exceeded, and (2) a 
17 
penalty ratchet, which applies when such exceedances occur repeatedly. 
18 
Q. 
What is the base penalty charge? 
19 
A. 
[Hammer] As described in more detail below, when an Eligible Customer taking service 
20 
on behalf of Co-Located Load exceeds its reserved transmission service limit, the base 
21 
penalty charge will be assessed for any hour in which at least one five-minute interval 
22 
occurs during which a customer’s telemetered load at the Point of Delivery exceeds its 
23

Exhibit No. PTO-0005 
Page 7 of 31 
reserved transmission service limit. This five-minute interval is defined as an Exceedance 
1 
Interval, and such an hour is defined as an Exceedance Hour. The base penalty charge will 
2 
apply to each Exceedance Hour.  
3 
Q. 
What is the penalty rachet? 
4 
A. 
[Hammer] As described in more detail below, the penalty rachet applies when multiple 
5 
Exceedance Hours occur during a particular time period. It is designed to discourage 
6 
recurring reliance on unreserved transmission capacity. Under the penalty rachet 
7 
framework, the penalty charges escalate as the frequency of unreserved transmission use 
8 
increases. Specifically, if more than one Exceedance Hour occurs on the same calendar 
9 
day, an additional daily penalty applies. If exceedances occur on multiple calendar days 
10 
within the same calendar week, an additional weekly penalty applies. Likewise, if 
11 
exceedances occur in multiple calendar weeks within the same month, an additional 
12 
monthly penalty applies, and if exceedances occur in multiple months within the same year, 
13 
an additional yearly penalty applies. By progressively increasing the economic 
14 
consequences of repeated penalties, the penalty ratchet reinforces the expectation that 
15 
Eligible Customers taking service on behalf of Co-Located Load customers manage their 
16 
load in a manner consistent with their reserved transmission service. 
17 
Base Penalty Charge 
18 
Q. 
Please describe the base penalty charge in more detail. 
19 
A. 
[Hammer] The base penalty charge will be assessed for any hour in which at least one 
20 
five-minute interval occurs during which a customer’s telemetered load at the Point of 
21 
Delivery exceeds its reserved transmission service limit. Such a five-minute interval is 
22 
defined as an Exceedance Interval, and such an hour is defined as an Exceedance Hour. 
23

Exhibit No. PTO-0005 
Page 8 of 31 
The base penalty charge will apply to each Exceedance Hour. For purposes of determining 
1 
whether one or more exceedances have occurred, each five-minute interval beginning with 
2 
the first minute of each hour shall constitute a separate interval.  Similarly, each hour from 
3 
0100 through 2400 shall constitute a separate hour. I explain the calculation of the reserved 
4 
transmission service limit and the base penalty charge in the following questions. 
5 
Q. 
How is the reserved transmission service limit determined? 
6 
A. 
[Hammer] For an Eligible Customer taking only Firm Contract Demand Service, the 
7 
reserved transmission service limit will equal the Firm Contract Demand minus any  
8 
curtailed MW.  For an Eligible Customer taking only Non-Firm Contract Demand Service, 
9 
the reserved transmission service limit will equal the approved Non-Firm Contract Demand 
10 
minus any curtailed MW. For an Eligible Customer taking Firm Contract Demand Service 
11 
and Non-Firm Contract Demand Service, the reserved transmission service limit will equal 
12 
the Firm Contract Demand plus the approved Non-Firm Contract Demand minus any 
13 
curtailed MW.  For an Eligible Customer taking Interim NITS, the reserved transmission 
14 
service limit will equal the Interim NITS demand minus any curtailed MW. 
15 
Q. 
How is the base penalty charge applied to each Exceedance Hour? 
16 
A. 
[Hammer] Under the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposal, the base penalty charge will 
17 
be applied to each Exceedance Hour and will be calculated as: 
18 
Hourly Exceedance MW × Equivalent Hourly Firm Contract Demand (“FCD”) rate × 
19 
number of Exceedance Intervals within the hour 
20 
Where: 
21 

Hourly Exceedance MW = Maximum telemetered load during the hour – Reserved 
22 
Transmission Service Limit for the hour 
23

Exhibit No. PTO-0005 
Page 9 of 31 

Equivalent Hourly FCD rate = FCD rate / 8,760 hours 
1 
Q. 
Why is the Firm Contract Demand Rate used as the basis for assessing the penalty? 
2 
A. 
[Hammer] The Firm Contract Demand rate is used as the basis for assessing the penalty 
3 
because, when a customer exceeds its reserved transmission service limit without 
4 
authorization, the excess usage effectively imposes firm‑level demand on the system. In 
5 
effect, the customer utilizes transmission facilities in the same manner as a firm load. 
6 
Q. 
Can you provide an example to illustrate the application of the base penalty charge 
7 
concept? 
8 
A. 
[Hammer] Yes. The following example demonstrates the application of the base penalty 
9 
charge concept.  This example is a hypothetical for illustration purposes only. 
10 
Firm Contract Demand (“FCD”) Rate is $72,000/MW-Year.  
11 
12 

Equivalent Monthly FCD Rate: $6,000/MW-Month 
13 

Equivalent Weekly FCD Rate: $1,385/MW-Week 
14 

Equivalent Daily FCD Rate: $197.26/MW-Day 
15 

Equivalent Hourly FCD Rate: $8.22/MW-Hour 
16 
17 
April 7, during Houring Ending (“HE”) 12:00 p.m., a Firm Contract Demand customer has 
18 
a total load of 500 MW and on-site generation of 400 MW. The customer has 100 MW 
19 
FCD and no approved Non-Firm Contract Demand for the hour. 
20 
21 
At 11:17 a.m., the customer experiences a sudden trip of 400 MW of on‑site generation. 
22 
While internal power controls immediately begin ramping down load and transferring 
23 
supply to backup generation, there is a brief delay before the protection systems fully 
24 
respond. As a result, the customer draws approximately 300 MW from the transmission 
25 
system for a period of seven minutes, from 11:17 a.m. to 11:24 a.m. (i.e., spanning two 
26 
five-minute intervals (11:15-11:20 a.m. and 11:20-11:25 a.m.)). 
27 
28 
Because the customer’s telemetered load exceeded its 100 MW of reserved transmission 
29 
service limit during the HE 12:00 p.m., the HE 12:00 p.m. qualifies as an Exceedance Hour, 
30 
triggering a financial penalty. 
31 
32 
For HE 12:00 p.m.: 
33 

Maximum telemetered load = 300 MW 
34 

Reserved Transmission Service Limit = 100 MW 
35 

Hourly Exceedance MW = 300 MW – 100 MW = 200 MW 
36

Exhibit No. PTO-0005 
Page 10 of 31 

Hourly FCD Rate = $8.22/MW‑Hour 
1 

Number of Exceedance Intervals during the hour = 2  
2 
3 
Base Penalty Charge for the HE 12:00 p.m.: 
4 
= 200 MW × $8.22/MW‑Hour x 2  
5 
= $3,288 
6 
7 
This penalty charge is in addition to the customer’s existing obligation to pay for its 100 
8 
MW of FCD under its transmission service agreement. 
9 
10 
Penalty Ratchet 
11 
Q. 
Please describe the penalty ratchet in more detail.
12 
A. 
[Hammer] The PJM Transmission Owners’ also propose a penalty ratchet to address 
13 
repeated exceedance behavior based on the frequency of unreserved use of the transmission 
14 
system. This penalty rachet is designed to discourage recurring reliance on unreserved 
15 
transmission capacity. Under this framework, the penalty rate escalates as the frequency of 
16 
unreserved transmission use increases. By progressively increasing the economic 
17 
consequences of repeated exceedances, the penalty ratchet reinforces the expectation that 
18 
Eligible Customers manage their Co-Located Load in a manner consistent with their 
19 
reserved transmission service limits. 
20 
Q. 
Can you explain the overall mechanics of the penalty ratchet? 
21 
A. 
[Hammer] Yes. The penalty ratchet is based on an Eligible Customer’s exceedance pattern 
22 
and applies escalating FCD–equivalent rates as the frequency of unreserved transmission 
23 
use increases. Depending on whether exceedances occur within the same calendar day, 
24 
calendar week, calendar month, or calendar year, the penalty ratchet applies daily, weekly, 
25 
monthly, or annual penalty charges, respectively. Below is an overview of the penalty 
26 
ratchet: 
27 
28

1 
Daily Penalty Charge 
2 
3 
Q.  
When does the Daily Penalty Charge apply, and how is it calculated? 
4 
A.  
[Hammer] The Daily Penalty Charge applies when multiple Exceedance Hours occur on 
5 
the same calendar day. In that circumstance, the Daily Penalty Charge is calculated as: 
6 
Maximum Hourly Exceedance MW during the calendar day 
7 
× Daily FCD-Equivalent Rate 
8 
× Number of Exceedance Hours in the calendar day 
9 
10 
Q. 
 Can you provide an example of the Daily Penalty Charge? 
11 
A.   
[Hammer] Using the same example as in the base penalty charge section, assume the 
12 
customer exceeds its reserved transmission service limit in two separate hours on the same 
13 
calendar day (one exceedance at 10:30 a.m. and another at 11:15 p.m.). As I explained 
14 
above, each clock hour will be treated as a separate hour for purposes of this determination, 
15 
so even though these exceedances occurred within an hour of each other, they will be 
16 
treated as two Exceedance Hours. In that case: 
17 

Maximum Exceedance MW during the calendar day = 200 MW 
18 

Daily FCD Rate = $197.26/MW‑Day 
19 

Number of Exceedance Hours in the calendar day = 2  
20 
21 
Daily Penalty Charge is calculated as: 
22 
23 
200 MW× $197.26/MW‑Day x 2  
24 
= $78,904 
25 
26 
The Daily Penalty Charge is assessed in addition to the base penalty charge applicable to 
27 
each individual Exceedance Hour. 
28

Weekly Penalty Charge 
1 
2 
Q.  
When does the Weekly Penalty Charge apply, and how is it calculated? 
3 
A.  
[Hammer] The Weekly Penalty Charge applies when Exceedance Hours occur on multiple 
4 
calendar days within the same calendar week. The Weekly Penalty Charge is calculated as: 
5 
Maximum Hourly Exceedance MW during the calendar week 
6 
× Weekly FCD-Equivalent Rate 
7 
× Number of Exceedance Days in the calendar week 
8 
9 
Q.  
Can you provide an example of the Weekly Penalty Charge?
10 
A.  
[Hammer] Using the same example, assume the customer exceeds its reserved 
11 
transmission service limit in two different calendar days (Monday and Wednesday) within 
12 
the same calendar week. In that case:
13 

Maximum Hourly Exceedance MW during the calendar week = 200 MW 
14 

Weekly FCD Rate= $1,385/MW‑Week 
15 

Number of Exceedance Days in a calendar week = 2  
16 
17 
Weekly Penalty Charge is calculated as: 
18 
19

20 
= $554,000 
21 
22

23 
applicable Daily Penalty Charge.

25 
26 
Q.  
When does the Monthly Penalty Charge apply, and how is it calculated?
27 
A.  
[Hammer] The Monthly Penalty Charge applies when Exceedance Hours occur during 
28 
multiple calendar weeks within the same calendar month. The Monthly Penalty Charge is 
29 
calculated as:
30 
Maximum Hourly Exceedance MW during the calendar month 
31

32

2

[Hammer] Using the same example, assume the customer exceeds its reserved 
3 
transmission service limit in two separate calendar weeks within the same calendar month. 
4 
In that case: 
5 


15

17

Q.  
When does the Annual Penalty Charge apply, and how is it calculated?
19 
A.  
[Hammer] The Annual Penalty Charge applies when Exceedance Hours occur during 
20 
multiple calendar months within the same calendar year. The Annual Penalty Charge is 
21 
calculated as: 
22 
Maximum Hourly Exceedance MW during the calendar year 
23

24

Can you provide an example of the Annual Penalty Charge? 
27 
A.  
[Hammer] Using the same example, assume the same customer exceeds its reserved 
28 
transmission service limit in two separate months within the same year. In that case: 
29 

Maximum Hourly Exceedance MW during a calendar year = 200 MW 
30 

FCD Rate = $72,000/MW‑Year 
31

5

6 
Q. 
What is the total penalty exposure under the calculations above? 
7 
A. 
[Hammer] In aggregate, if the Eligible Customer experiences two Exceedance Intervals 
8 
within a single hour, two hours within a single calendar day, two calendar days within a 
9 
single calendar week, and two calendar weeks within the same calendar month during two 
10 
months of the year (e.g., April and May), the total assessed financial penalty would be 
11 
approximately $36.5 million. The calculation supporting this total is summarized as
